spec.genre: reflective essay on a hobby or craft
spec.theme: book swaps as a response to shrinking school library budgets

blueprint.speaker: Dell Hartigan, a retired bookbinder and parent volunteer who has run a monthly book swap at Corbett Hollow Middle School for five years
blueprint.audience: Parents and townspeople of Corbett Hollow who read the community newsletter, including some who watch school board decisions and some who regard the swap as a trivial stopgap
blueprint.exigence: The fifth anniversary of the swap, arriving as the school board prepares to vote again on the library budget
blueprint.purpose: To reframe the swap as a craft with its own lessons, to insist that it is not a substitute for a funded library, and to argue that it teaches children a habit of giving books that will outlast the budget vote
blueprint.context: Six years earlier the district cut the library purchasing allowance and reduced the librarian to part time; the writer began the swap in response
blueprint.claim: The book swap is best understood not as charity or as a replacement for the library but as a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along, a habit that will outlast whichever way the budget vote goes
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 narrates the first swap and names the thesis (craft, not charity). Paragraph 2 supplies the exigence: the budget cut and its slow effect. Paragraph 3 asks what a swap does and answers with the handling: sorting, mending, keeping a ledger, and the lesson of slowness. Paragraph 4 concedes what the swap cannot do and refuses to let the board use it as an excuse. Paragraph 5 pivots to the one thing the swap does that the library never did: it makes givers of books, illustrated by an anecdote. Paragraph 6 qualifies the scale of the swap, then closes with the antithesis that a craft need not be large to be serious and that the habit will outlast the vote.

tone_shifts.to: reflective, inquisitive description of the craft

set.title: Take One, Leave One
paragraphs: The first swap, five Octobers ago, fit on two folding tables borrowed from the cafeteria at Corbett Hollow Middle School.
I brought forty-one books from my own shelves, most of them paperbacks with cracked spines, and a sign made from the back of a cereal box that said, in marker, Take One, Leave One, No Questions.
By the end of the lunch period the tables held fifty-three books, which is to say the children had done the arithmetic in our favor without being asked.
I have been running the swap every month since, and I have come to think of it less as a charity than as a craft, something with its own tools and its own slow lessons.
The reason the swap exists is not mysterious.

When the district trimmed its budget six years ago, the library's purchasing allowance fell from roughly nine thousand dollars a year to just over one thousand, and the librarian, Mrs. Avendale, went from full time to two days a week.
A thousand dollars buys perhaps sixty new hardcovers, in a building with four hundred and ten students.
The shelves did not empty overnight; they simply stopped growing, the way a town stops growing when the last factory closes and nobody notices until the graduating class is half its old size.
New titles arrived in children's conversations but not in the catalog, and the gap between what they wanted to read and what they could find became a kind of quiet weather in the building.
So what, exactly, does a book swap do that a shelf of donations in the front office does not?
The answer is in the handling.
Every month I sort what comes in, mend what can be mended with linen tape and a bone folder, and set aside what is beyond saving for the art teacher, who turns the pages into collage.
I keep a ledger, a spiral notebook, nothing grand, in which I write down what left the table and what came back.

The ledger has taught me more about the reading life of this town than any survey could: which series travel in packs, which single battered copy has passed through nine households, which eighth grader keeps bringing in horse novels she has outgrown so that someone younger can have them.
Mending is slow.
Sorting is slow.
That slowness is the point, because a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly for a long time, and the children who help me have learned it alongside me.
I should be honest about what the swap cannot do.
It cannot buy the new book everyone is talking about; it can only wait for someone to tire of it.
It cannot catalog, cannot teach a sixth grader to find a source, cannot do the hundred invisible things Mrs. Avendale does in her two days.
A table of secondhand paperbacks is not a library, and anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse.
I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow and put me out of business.
And yet.
There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did: it makes children into givers of books rather than only borrowers of them.
A borrowed book is returned because it must be; a swapped book is released because somebody decided another reader should have it.

I have watched a boy stand at the table for most of a lunch period deciding whether he could part with a dog-eared fantasy novel, and I have watched him come back the next month to ask whether anyone took it.
Someone had.
He seemed, if anything, pleased, the way you are pleased to hear that a letter arrived.
I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is.
It is two tables and a notebook and a roll of linen tape, and on a bad month it is forty books and a rainy lunch period.
But a craft does not have to be large to be serious, and a town does not have to be rich to teach its children that books are things you pass along rather than things you wait to be given.
The budget may come back; I hope it does.
The habit, I suspect, will outlast whichever way the vote goes.

spec.theme: the ethics of crowdfunding for medical bills

blueprint.speaker: Teodor Brandvik, a longtime columnist for the fictional Harrow County Ledger who knew Lenore Quist personally
blueprint.audience: Residents of Pell's Landing and the surrounding county who read the paper and, in many cases, donated to Lenore's fundraising page
blueprint.exigence: The death of Lenore Quist, a beloved school bus driver, after a widely shared medical crowdfunding campaign raised 53,400 dollars; the town is celebrating the figure, and the columnist feels the celebration hides an uncomfortable truth
blueprint.purpose: To honor Lenore sincerely while arguing that the success of her campaign, set beside a neighbor's failed one, exposes a system that rations care by popularity, and to redirect the readers' generosity toward a demand for structural change
blueprint.context: An obituary-style tribute column in a small-town newspaper, written within a week of the death, addressed to a community that regards the fundraising total as a point of pride
blueprint.claim: Crowdfunding gave Lenore real money and real comfort, but a system in which the sick must audition for survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to neighbors, and the community's kindness should not be mistaken for justice
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 establishes Lenore's character through concrete anecdote and sets up the tension between honoring the figure and telling the truth. P2 narrates the campaign's success and the warmth behind it. P3 shifts tone and introduces the contrasting case of Aurelio Dansk, whose nearly identical situation raised almost nothing, isolating popularity as the deciding variable. P4 concedes the real benefits of the page, then rebuts with the lifeboat/harbor metaphor and the central claim about outsourced stinginess. P5 supplies the charity/justice distinction that explains why confusing the two makes the Aurelios invisible. P6 returns to direct address, asking donors to remember both Lenore and the fact that the burden should never have fallen on them.

tone_shifts.to: intimate, direct exhortation to the readers

blueprint.counterargument: Defenders of crowdfunding pages say the money is real and the comfort is real, and that donors do something good; the writer concedes both fully, then argues that a lifeboat is not a harbor and that the system has merely outsourced its stinginess to neighbors.

planned_flaws.flaw: The admission that Lenore would have disliked the column slightly risks undercutting the writer's authority to speak for her

provenance.note: Entirely fictional tribute column; all names, places and figures invented.

set.title: The Number Seven Bus
paragraphs: Lenore Quist drove the number seven bus for the Pell's Landing schools for twenty-two years and never once left a child at the curb because the clock said she could.
She kept a shoebox of spare mittens under the driver's seat.
She knew which kids needed a louder good morning and which needed none at all.

When she died last Tuesday, at fifty-eight, of the kidney disease that had been chasing her for two years, the town did what towns do: it brought casseroles, lowered the flag at the depot, and opened the fundraising page one more time to see the final figure.
Fifty-three thousand, four hundred dollars.
I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath.
The page went up in March of last year, built by her niece at the kitchen table while Lenore protested from the next room that she did not want her face on the internet.
The niece won.
The photograph showed Lenore in her reflective vest, one hand on the folding door, grinning at someone out of frame.

Within nine days the page passed its first goal; within a month it had covered the share of dialysis the insurance would not, the gas to a clinic forty miles away, and three months of rent she lost when she could no longer sit behind the wheel.
People she had driven as six-year-olds, now with mortgages of their own, wrote notes beneath their donations.
One simply said: you waited for me in the snow.
Here is the part the eulogies have skipped.
Four streets over lived a man named Aurelio Dansk, a night-shift machinist with the same disease, the same clinic, and the same forty-mile drive.
His page, which his daughter built with the same template, raised eleven hundred dollars.
He was not less sick, and he was not less deserving, unless we have quietly decided that deserving means being known, being photographed well, and having driven half the county's children to school.
He was simply a man whom fewer people had met, and the arithmetic of charity is pitiless about that.
I will concede what the defenders of these pages say, because it is true: the money was real, and so was the comfort.
Lenore read every note aloud, and her niece told me that on the worst mornings the page was the first thing she opened, before the pill organizer, before the coffee.
Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely.
But a lifeboat is not a harbor, and we should stop describing the boat as though it were the shore.
A system in which the sick must audition for their own survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to the kindness of neighbors and then taken credit for the kindness.
There is an old distinction worth reviving here, between charity and justice.
Charity is what one person chooses to give; justice is what no person should have to ask for.
When we blur the two, letting the warmth of the first stand in for the absence of the second, we make the Aurelios of the world invisible and the Lenores into proof that the arrangement works.
It does not work.
It worked for her, for a while, because she was a story that was easy to tell, and even that was not enough in the end.
So here is what I would ask you to remember, you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred.
Remember the mittens, the snow, the grin at the folding door.
Remember also that you were asked, out of your own pockets and on nine days' notice, to do something that should never have fallen to you at all.
Lenore would have disliked this column; she hated being made an example of.
But she waited for every child, including the ones nobody else was watching for, and I can think of no better instruction for the rest of us.

options.why: Paragraph 5 adds no new evidence about Aurelio; it refers to the Aurelios of the world as a category and works by definition rather than by fresh example.

options.text: Paragraph 4 defines the terms the argument depends on, and paragraph 5 applies those terms to the specific cases of Lenore and Aurelio introduced earlier
options.label: reversal
options.why: The definitions of charity and justice appear in paragraph 5, not paragraph 4; the order of the two functions is reversed.

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes the real benefits of the page before declaring the system inadequate, and paragraph 5 supplies a distinction that explains why confusing those benefits with a remedy causes harm
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 moves from concession to the lifeboat metaphor and the central claim; paragraph 5 then defines charity and justice and shows that blurring them makes the Aurelios invisible, giving the claim its conceptual grounding.

options.text: Paragraph 4 condemns the donors for mistaking a boat for the shore, and paragraph 5 softens that condemnation by admitting that the arrangement did in fact work for Lenore
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 4 explicitly says nobody who gave did anything wrong, and the admission in paragraph 5 that it worked for her for a while is immediately qualified as not enough, not a retraction.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer develops the discussion of Aurelio Dansk primarily through

options.text: comparison of two closely matched cases, which allows the writer to isolate recognition as the one factor that explains the difference in outcomes
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lists what Aurelio shared with Lenore (disease, clinic, drive, template) and then names the single difference, that fewer people had met him; the matched comparison makes the conclusion about charity's arithmetic feel earned.

options.text: classification of patients into those who are well known and those who are not, which lets the writer propose a fairer system of allocating aid
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer works with two individuals rather than categories here, and no alternative system of allocation is proposed anywhere in the passage.

options.text: a cause-and-effect sequence showing that Lenore's successful campaign drew donations away from Aurelio's and left him with less
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The paragraph does explain why Aurelio raised less, but it never claims Lenore's page took money from his; the cause named is simply that fewer people knew him.

options.text: narration of Aurelio's illness and his daughter's efforts, which deepens the reader's sympathy for a patient the eulogies ignored
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph gives almost no narrative of Aurelio's illness; it withholds story deliberately, and its aim is analytic rather than sympathetic.

items.stem: In the sentence beginning "A system in which the sick must audition" in paragraph 4, the semicolon primarily serves to

options.text: signal that the second clause reports what the defenders of these pages say, which the writer has promised to concede
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The defenders' view was stated and conceded earlier with a colon; the clause after the semicolon is the writer's own indictment, not reported speech.

options.text: separate the items in a list of the system's failures, each of which the writer has documented in the preceding paragraphs
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The semicolon joins two independent clauses, not list items; the clause that follows is a single claim with its own subject and verbs.

options.text: introduce a pause that softens the accusation against the system by giving readers a moment to absorb the writer's concession
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The concession ended in the previous sentences; this sentence is the rebuttal, and the semicolon tightens rather than softens the accusation.

options.text: bind the rejection of the word generous directly to the correction that replaces it, so the second clause reads as an immediate verdict on the first
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins the negative judgment (is not generous) and the positive account (has outsourced its stinginess) without a conjunction, so the substitution lands at once rather than as a separate afterthought.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the statement "Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely" most directly addresses the audience's

options.text: likely fear that a critique of the fundraising page is also an accusation against the people who donated to it
options.label: correct
options.why: The audience includes donors (paragraph 6 addresses 'you who gave'); before the writer attacks the system, this sentence reassures donors that they are not the target, keeping them receptive to the rebuttal that follows in 'But a lifeboat is not a harbor.'

options.text: assumption that the critique in paragraph 3 was mistaken and that Lenore's page was simply more deserving
options.label: reversal
options.why: Far from retracting paragraph 3, the writer immediately pivots with 'But' to the lifeboat metaphor and the claim about outsourced stinginess; the praise of donors sets up the critique rather than withdrawing it.

options.text: suspicion that the writer, as a friend of Lenore, is too close to the story to judge the campaign fairly
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence is about the donors' conduct, not the writer's credibility; the writer's closeness to Lenore is handled elsewhere (paragraph 6) and this sentence makes no claim about his own objectivity.

options.text: expectation that the column will ask them to give again, this time to the page built for Aurelio Dansk
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never asks readers to donate to Aurelio's page or to anyone; paragraph 6 asks only that they remember, and the passage's demand is structural, not for a second collection.

items.stem: The writer's phrasing "you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred" in paragraph 6 most likely serves to

options.text: rebuke readers whose gifts were too small to cover the dialysis costs and the lost rent described in paragraph 2
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone of paragraph 6 is tender and grateful ('Remember the mittens'); the writer's complaint is that readers were asked at all, not that they gave too little.

options.text: include every donor in the final request regardless of amount, treating the readers as ordinary neighbors rather than wealthy benefactors
options.label: correct
options.why: The range of modest sums names the typical reader as a small-scale giver and makes the address inclusive, so the instruction to 'Remember' and 'Remember also' lands on the whole community of donors the column is aimed at.

options.text: demonstrate that the writer tracked each donation closely enough to know what individual readers had contributed
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The two figures are illustrative round amounts, not a record; the passage gives no indication the writer reviewed individual donations, and the phrase works as a general address, not as evidence of research.

options.text: suggest that the smaller contributions mattered less to the final total than the larger ones listed on the page
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nothing ranks donors by size; the pairing puts twenty and two hundred on equal footing, and the passage elsewhere treats the collective giving as the point, not individual sums.

items.stem: The niece's report in paragraph 4 that on the worst mornings the page "was the first thing she opened, before the pill organizer, before the coffee" is used chiefly to support the writer's acknowledgment that

options.text: the comfort the page gave Lenore was as real as the money it raised
options.label: correct
options.why: The detail directly follows the concession 'the money was real, and so was the comfort' and illustrates that comfort concretely, showing the page's emotional value before the writer turns to his rebuttal.

options.text: Lenore would have disliked being made an example of in a public column
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Her reluctance about publicity appears in paragraphs 2 and 6, but the detail here shows her eagerly reading the page, which if anything cuts the other way; it is not offered for that claim.

options.text: a system that makes the sick audition for survival has outsourced its stinginess
options.label: partially_right
options.why: That claim is the writer's rebuttal later in the same paragraph; the niece's detail belongs to the concession the writer grants before 'But,' and it does not demonstrate stinginess.

options.text: the campaign covered dialysis costs, clinic travel, and three months of lost rent
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Those financial results are established in paragraph 2 with the timeline of goals; the morning ritual is about emotional sustenance, not what the money paid for.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "It worked for her, for a while, because she was a story that was easy to tell, and even that was not enough in the end" qualifies the preceding claim "It does not work" primarily by

options.text: restricting the critique to cases of kidney disease, where the clinic's distance made costs unusually hard to meet
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Nothing in the sentence limits the claim to a disease or to travel costs; the argument throughout is about who gets known and funded, not about a particular illness.

options.text: shifting responsibility onto Lenore by implying she cultivated a public image that drew donations away from others
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage shows Lenore resisting publicity ('she did not want her face on the internet'); being 'a story that was easy to tell' describes how others saw her, not anything she did.

options.text: withdrawing the denial by granting that the arrangement does function reliably for people who are widely known in their communities
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence does not say the system works for the well known; it says it worked 'for a while' and 'even that was not enough,' which denies reliability rather than granting it.

options.text: admitting a temporary exception while attributing it to Lenore's appeal as a story rather than to the arrangement itself, so the denial is honest but still stands
options.label: correct
options.why: The qualification concedes 'for her, for a while,' but the reason given, that she was 'easy to tell,' isolates popularity as the cause, and 'not enough in the end' closes the exception, so the indictment survives intact.

items.stem: The final sentence of paragraph 1, "I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath," previews the organization of the column by

options.text: forecasting a comparison between the two fundraising templates used by Lenore's niece and Aurelio's daughter
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The identical template is a single detail in paragraph 3 used to rule out a variable; the sentence previews honoring versus truth-telling, a far broader frame than the pages' design.

options.text: announcing two tasks that the column then takes in sequence, tribute to Lenore and the campaign first, critique of what the figure conceals afterward
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 honor Lenore and narrate the page's success; paragraph 3 opens 'Here is the part the eulogies have skipped' and turns to truth-telling, so the sentence forecasts the two-part movement and the tension between them.

options.text: signaling that the writer will decline to honor the figure at all, since honesty about it makes celebration impossible
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly wants to honor the figure and does so, returning in paragraph 6 to 'the mittens, the snow, the grin'; the doubt is about doing both at once, not about refusing one.

options.text: promising a chronological account of Lenore's illness from the first diagnosis through the final week before her death
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The column is organized by argument, not by medical timeline; after paragraph 2 it leaves Lenore's story to compare Aurelio's case and define charity against justice.

items.stem: The placement of the sentence "Here is the part the eulogies have skipped" at the opening of paragraph 3 primarily serves to

options.text: mark the turn from tribute to critique and set the column apart from the conventional memorials it has resembled so far
options.label: correct
options.why: After two paragraphs of warm narration, this sentence announces omitted material and introduces Aurelio Dansk, shifting the tone to confrontation and distinguishing the column from the eulogies.

options.text: introduce evidence that the eulogies overstated the total raised on Lenore's fundraising page
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never disputes the 53,400 dollar figure; what the eulogies skipped is Aurelio's parallel case, not an error in Lenore's total.

options.text: dismiss the preceding praise of Lenore as sentimental and insincere in light of her neighbor's experience
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never retracts the tribute; paragraph 6 repeats it ('Remember the mittens'), and paragraph 4 insists the donors 'did... something lovely.' The sentence adds to the story rather than discrediting it.

options.text: summarize the account of the campaign's success in paragraph 2 before the writer moves on to its financial details
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence looks forward to something new ('the part... skipped'), not back; the financial details of Lenore's campaign have already been given in paragraph 2.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the structure of the sentence "Charity is what one person chooses to give; justice is what no person should have to ask for" chiefly emphasizes the relationship between the two ideas by

options.text: making the second clause noticeably longer to signal that justice is the more complicated and contested of the two concepts
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The clauses are nearly equal in length and the passage never calls justice complicated; its point is that justice is simply what should not have to be requested.

options.text: placing the two terms in identical clause frames so that the contrast falls on the few words that differ: who acts and whether the act is voluntary
options.label: correct
options.why: Both clauses follow the pattern 'X is what... person...,' so the differences, 'one' versus 'no' and 'chooses to give' versus 'should have to ask for,' carry the whole distinction the next sentence builds on.

options.text: balancing the two clauses so evenly that the terms appear interchangeable, preparing the reader to accept the blurring the writer describes
options.label: reversal
options.why: The balance sharpens the difference rather than erasing it; the following sentence treats blurring the two as the error that makes 'the Aurelios of the world invisible.'

options.text: subordinating the clause about justice to the clause about charity so that justice appears to follow as a consequence of giving
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are coordinate, joined by a semicolon with neither dependent on the other; the passage argues charity cannot substitute for justice, not that one produces the other.

blueprint.purpose: To persuade garden members to approve a signal booster and study table at the garden shed so students without home internet can do homework

blueprint.theme: rural broadband and the homework gap

provenance.venue_alias: Hollis Creek Community Garden bulletin board

set.title: Homework at the Garden Fence
paragraphs: Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on.
Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all.
Internet is important for students these days.
My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring.
Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar.
My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot.
Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.
The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply.
A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell.
A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car.
The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.
Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind.
Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night.
I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

items.stem: Many garden members are retirees who keep a close eye on the committee's small budget. The writer wants to revise sentence 9 to address this audience's concern about cost. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, which is honestly nothing compared to what a good education is worth.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the members' budget worry instead of addressing it.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, less than last summer's new hoses, and my family has offered to pay half.
options.label: correct
options.why: Puts the cost in terms members know and reduces the burden on the budget, directly answering their concern.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, and it would probably pay for itself many times over someday.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a vague, unsupported financial claim that does not reassure budget-minded readers.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof, a model with two antennas and a weatherproof case, is sold at the hardware co-op in Pell.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds product details but drops the cost entirely, ignoring the audience's concern.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that respects members who finished school without the internet while explaining why students today cannot do the same. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Today the assignments exist only online, and the school stopped handing out printed packets two years ago.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Explains the change but does not acknowledge members who studied without the internet.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, which shows that the old way was always better for kids.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Undercuts the writer's own argument instead of explaining why students now need internet.

options.text: Many of you probably think kids today are lazy and just want to sit on their phones at the garden fence.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Assumes the worst of readers rather than respecting them, and explains nothing.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, but today the assignments themselves exist only online.
options.label: correct
options.why: Honors members' experience and explains the change that makes their approach impossible now.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals a second, separate improvement following the one described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For instance,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Presents the table as an example of the booster, which it is not.

options.text: In contrast,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals opposition, but the table complements the booster.

options.text: As a result,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly implies the booster causes the table to exist.

options.text: In addition,
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals that the table is a further improvement added to the booster.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 13 with a transition that shows the sentence is a response to the worry raised in sentence 12. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Similarly to that concern,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, but sentence 13 answers rather than resembles the worry.

options.text: To address that concern,
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly marks sentence 13 as the answer to the members' worry.

options.text: Despite that small concern,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Belittles the members' worry and suggests the writer will disregard it.

options.text: Because of that concern,
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions the concern but frames the promise as merely caused by it, not as a reply.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that ends the flyer by reminding garden members that the proposal fits values they already hold as growers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: This garden has always shared its extra seedlings and spare tools with neighbors, and a table and a stronger signal would just be one more thing we share.
options.label: correct
options.why: Ties the proposal to the members' existing habit of sharing, so the ending appeals to values they already hold.

options.text: High-speed internet is now a basic need across the country, and every rural community will have to deal with the gap sooner or later.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves away from this garden and its members' values to a general national claim.

options.text: If the vote fails, students will keep failing quizzes like Caleb did, and the committee will have to explain why it let that happen.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Ends on a threat that blames the readers instead of appealing to their values.

options.text: The signal booster from the co-op in Pell can be installed in about an afternoon by any member who owns a sturdy ladder.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a practical detail rather than a closing appeal to shared values.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that makes an arguable claim and previews both the proposal and the response to members' concerns. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For about 140 dollars and a picnic table, the garden could give ridge students a warm, connected place to study without harming a single plot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim, previews the booster and the table, and answers the worry about the plots.

options.text: Many families on Marrow Ridge still have no internet service at home, which makes school harder for their children this fall.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: States a situation, not an arguable claim, and previews no proposal; the passage also never shows that many families lack service.

options.text: The garden should buy a signal booster for the shed roof so that its Wi-Fi reaches farther into the gravel lot.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Previews only the booster and leaves out the study table and the concerns about the plots.

options.text: Rural internet access is one of the most important problems facing students, parents, and teachers in the county.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Too general; it does not name the garden's proposal at all.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how Caleb's experience supports the claim that students need a reliable connection. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: He knew the material, but a weak signal kept him from practicing it, so the connection decided his grade more than his effort did.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains how the anecdote shows that unreliable access, not ability, hurt his grade.

options.text: Caleb is a junior this year and hopes to study nursing at a college somewhere in the state after he graduates.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background about Caleb that has nothing to do with the claim.

options.text: Chemistry is widely considered one of the hardest subjects in high school, especially for students who struggle with math.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the subject was the problem, which works against the point about the connection.

options.text: His mother has since switched to a different phone plan, though the hotspot still drops out when it rains on the ridge.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions the connection again but does not explain how the example supports the claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 10 and 11 concisely, keeping the idea that the table would need no change to the garden's hours. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would give students a place besides a cold car and would need no new hours, since the garden already stays open until dusk.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concise and clear, and it keeps the causal link between the existing hours and needing no new ones.

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car, the garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice, and the last clause is a fragment.

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car, although the garden already stays open until dusk anyway.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "Although" signals contrast where there is none and leaves out the point about hours.

options.text: Because the garden already stays open until dusk, a picnic table and outlet under the awning would let students work somewhere besides a cold car at all hours.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Wrongly makes the hours the reason for the table, and "at all hours" contradicts closing at dusk.

set.title: Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters
paragraphs: Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there.
Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.
Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.
Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop.
At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University.
An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.
He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.
Arturo's story is not unusual.
Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else.
Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important.
Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.
Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.
Hope to see you there.

spec.theme: preserving a night market's character during redevelopment

blueprint.speaker: Teodora Vask, a writer who grew up working at her aunt's fried-noodle stall in the Halvern Street night market in the fictional port city of Orrisport
blueprint.audience: Members of the Orrisport Redevelopment Council and civically engaged residents reading the local journal during the public comment period on the market plan
blueprint.exigence: The Council has published a redevelopment plan that would replace the market's self-built stalls with a covered pavilion of sixty identical stalls and a 'curated vendor mix'; the comment period closes at the end of the month
blueprint.purpose: To persuade the Council to amend the plan so that it fixes safety hazards while leaving the stalls, vendor tenure, and informal customs intact
blueprint.context: A sixty-year-old informal night market that grew out of after-dark fish sales in the 1950s; a nearby market, Marrow Lane, was standardized in 2009 and lost its vendors and late hours
blueprint.claim: A market's character is not a look that can be designed but a set of habits held by particular people over a long time; a plan that standardizes stalls and reselects vendors will destroy what it claims to preserve, so the Council should repair hazards and leave the rest alone
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Opens with an anecdote of a blackout in which unorganized vendors lit lanterns in unison (par. 1), then traces the market's unplanned accretion (par. 2); summarizes the plan and concedes the safety problems are real before showing the plan goes far beyond safety (par. 3); offers Marrow Lane as a nearby precedent of the same approach failing (par. 4); defines character as habits rather than appearance, which explains why the precedent failed (par. 5); closes with a concrete alternative and direct appeal to the Council (par. 6)

Parallel 'that' clauses enumerate specific habits; parallel imperatives lay out the alternative plan

set.title: Where the Lanterns Are
paragraphs: On the night in 1987 when the power failed along Halvern Street, my aunt Ines kept frying.

She had a camping lantern under the counter, a habit from the years before the market had any wiring at all, and within ten minutes every stall on the block was lit the same way, forty small flames in a row like a procession that had decided to stand still.
Nobody organized that.
Nobody could have.
I think of those lanterns now because the Orrisport Redevelopment Council has published its plan for the market, and the plan is, above all, organized.
The Halvern Street market was never founded; it accumulated.
In the early 1950s, fishmongers from the quay began selling the day's unsold catch from handcarts after dark, and the people who bought from them wanted something to eat while they waited.
A woman named Pell Orano set a griddle on a crate.

Within a decade there were stalls built from salvaged doors, awnings stitched from sailcloth, and an unwritten system of rights by which a family's spot passed from parent to child without anyone ever signing a lease.
The city tolerated it, taxed it lightly, and for sixty years mostly left it alone.
The Council's plan would replace all of this with a covered pavilion of sixty identical stalls, a central payment kiosk, and what the document calls a "curated vendor mix."
I want to be fair to the people who wrote it.
The wiring on Halvern Street is a genuine hazard; I have seen extension cords running through puddles, and the drainage has not been improved since my aunt's time.
A market that electrocutes its customers has no character worth defending.
But the plan does not stop at the wiring.
It proposes to select which vendors return, to assign their positions by lottery, and to charge rents that the document itself admits will be "substantially above current informal levels."
We have seen this before, two miles away.
The Marrow Lane market was rebuilt in 2009 along almost exactly these lines: a handsome steel roof, uniform counters, a selection committee.
The ribbon was cut in May.

By the following winter, a third of the chosen vendors had given up their leases, the committee had filled the gaps with a coffee franchise and a shop selling scented candles, and the market closed, by ordinance, at nine o'clock.
Halvern Street does not close at nine.
It closes when the last cook is too tired to stand, which is a different kind of rule, and one no committee has ever managed to write down.
What the Council means by character, I suspect, is a look: the lanterns, the sailcloth, the handwritten signs that its renderings reproduce so lovingly.
But character, in a market, is not a look.

It is a set of habits held by particular people over a long time: the knowledge that Orano's grandson will take the corner because his grandmother took it, that a new vendor earns a spot by being tolerated at the edges for a season, that a dispute about a spilled bucket is settled by the oldest woman on the block and not by a kiosk.
You can photograph the sailcloth.
You cannot photograph the tolerance.
A pavilion can be built in eighteen months; the habits took sixty years, and they are not transferable to whoever wins a lottery.
None of this means the market should stay dangerous.
Fix the wiring; the vendors have asked for it since before I was born.
Lay proper drains.

Then leave the stalls where they are, grant the existing families the tenure they have always held in practice, and let the edges stay ragged enough for the next Pell Orano to set a griddle on a crate.
Council members, you have until the end of the month to amend this plan.
You can give Halvern Street a roof.
Make sure that when the lights go out beneath it, there is still someone who knows where the lanterns are.

spec.theme: the role of failure in learning a musical instrument

blueprint.speaker: Marisol Teague, a cellist who has taught adult students for eleven years at the fictional Pellam Falls Community Music School, writing a first-person feature essay
blueprint.audience: General magazine readers, particularly adults considering taking up an instrument and parents of young music students
blueprint.exigence: The school canceled its spring recital after most adult students who had signed up quietly stopped attending lessons, a pattern the writer has seen every year
blueprint.purpose: To persuade readers that adult learners quit not because they make mistakes but because they interpret mistakes as verdicts on themselves, and to show that teaching can change this interpretation
blueprint.context: A community music school in a small town; adult amateur music instruction; an annual recital cycle from September to spring
blueprint.claim: Learners abandon instruments not because they fail but because they hear each failure as a verdict rather than as information; teachers can and should train students to hear mistakes as messages
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 establishes the exigence and the puzzle (students leave without failing). Paragraph 2 gives a representative anecdote of a diligent student who quit after one wrong note. Paragraph 3 defines the key distinction between failure as verdict and failure as information. Paragraph 4 concedes that beginners cannot yet read the information in their mistakes, then turns that limitation into a responsibility for teachers. Paragraph 5 describes the writer's Wrong Note Wednesdays practice and its retention results. Paragraph 6 qualifies the claim, then shifts to direct address and closes by restating the verdict/message antithesis.

devices.function: Quantifies the dropout problem and later the retention effect of the Wednesday exercise
The tide simile conveys the inevitability and loss of the annual dropout; the mechanics simile conveys the calm, diagnostic attitude toward error
Ruth's story dramatizes a capable, diligent learner quitting over the interpretation of a single mistake
Very short sentences after longer ones land the key points with blunt emphasis
Legal metaphors (sentence, verdict, plead guilty) and the language metaphor frame the two ways of hearing failure
Explicitly defines failure as verdict versus failure as information
Balanced opposing clauses sharpen the verdict/information distinction
Matching structures make the two interpretations directly comparable
Admits beginners cannot read their mistakes, then reframes this as a reason to teach differently
Colons introduce concrete lists that ground abstract claims in specifics
Lists of specific actions and reasons add concreteness
Limits the claim so the exercise is not oversold
Turns to the reader as prospective learner or parent to apply the argument
Repeated 'verdict' and 'information/message' keep the central distinction before the reader
Establishes the writer's long teaching experience and hands-on practice

tone_shifts.to: direct, urging address to the reader

blueprint.counterargument: Beginners cannot read the information in their mistakes because they lack the skill to diagnose them, so the verdict/information distinction may be useless to those who need it most; the writer concedes the gap but argues it is a reason for teachers to do the translating aloud, not evidence that adults cannot learn

set.title: The Wrong Note Is Not the Verdict
paragraphs: In March the Pellam Falls Community Music School canceled its spring recital, and nobody was surprised except the people who had never taught there.
Of the forty-one adult students who had signed up in September to play a piece in front of an audience, fourteen remained by the first week of March.
The rest had not failed their lessons; most of them had been progressing on schedule.
They had simply stopped coming.
I have taught cello at the school for eleven years, and I have watched this happen every spring, like a tide that goes out and does not come back.
Consider Ruth Abernathy, a retired pharmacist who began lessons at fifty-eight because, as she told me, she was tired of being an audience.
For five months she was my most diligent student: she taped her fingerboard, counted aloud, and arrived early to tune.
Then one Tuesday in February, playing a simple shift from first position to fourth, she landed a half step flat and heard it.
She stopped, lowered the bow, and said, very quietly, "So that is what I sound like."
She did not come back.
The missed note had told her something true about her hand, but she heard it as a sentence passed on her whole person.
That distinction is the one I most want adult learners to understand, so let me draw it plainly.
A failure can be treated as a verdict, a judgment about who you are, or it can be treated as information, a report about what your hand did at a particular moment under particular conditions.
The verdict closes a case; the information opens one.
The verdict asks, "Am I musical?"; the information asks, "Was my elbow too low?"
Professional musicians are not people who have stopped making mistakes; they are people who have learned to hear a wrong note as a question rather than an answer.
I will grant that this is easier to say than to do, and that beginners face a genuine obstacle in doing it.
A flat note carries information only to someone with enough skill to read it, and a beginner, almost by definition, lacks that skill.
Ruth heard that the note was wrong; she could not yet hear why.
In that gap, where the ear is good enough to detect error but not yet good enough to diagnose it, the verdict rushes in to fill the silence.
But the gap is an argument for teaching differently, not an argument that adults cannot learn.
If the student cannot yet translate a mistake into instruction, then for a while the teacher must do the translating out loud, until the student learns the grammar.
Three years ago I began running what my students, not entirely kindly, call Wrong Note Wednesdays.
Once a week, each student plays a passage for the group with the deliberate goal of missing something: a shift, a rhythm, a string crossing.
The group then names what they heard, and the player names what the hand did.
There is no applause and no wincing, only a room full of adults saying "the thumb got left behind" with the calm of mechanics discussing a carburetor.
The exercise is faintly ridiculous, and the students know it.
Yet of the twenty-six students who have passed through the Wednesday group, twenty-two were still enrolled the following autumn, against a school-wide retention rate of roughly half.
They do not play better than the others, at least not at first.
They quit less.
I do not want to overstate what a Wednesday can do.
Some students leave for reasons no exercise can touch: a move, a diagnosis, a grandchild who needs the spare room where the cello lived.
And a practiced ear for one's own mistakes is not the same thing as talent, whatever talent is.

But if you are an adult thinking about picking up an instrument, or a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page, I would ask you to notice which kind of failure is on offer in the room.
If every wrong note is a verdict, the learner will eventually plead guilty and leave.
If every wrong note is a message, the learner may stay long enough to become fluent in the language, which is, after all, the only thing we ever meant by learning to play.

items.stem: The writer's portrayal of Ruth Abernathy in paragraph 2 most directly appeals to the audience by

options.text: demonstrating that common beginner habits such as taping the fingerboard and counting aloud are ineffective, so that readers seek more rigorous instruction methods
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The habits are listed to show Ruth's diligence, not to criticize them; the passage never evaluates the methods themselves.

options.text: presenting a diligent, steadily progressing adult whose departure cannot be blamed on effort or ability, so that readers who fear their own mistakes see quitting as a matter of interpretation
options.label: correct
options.why: Ruth is 'my most diligent student,' progressing for five months, and leaves after one flat note heard 'as a sentence passed on her whole person,' which locates the problem in interpretation, not capacity.

options.text: suggesting that adults who begin lessons late in life lack the ear required to distinguish a correct note from an incorrect one, so that readers lower their expectations
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ruth 'heard it' immediately; the passage says her ear detected the error, and the writer explicitly denies that the gap means adults cannot learn.

options.text: evoking sympathy for an older learner humiliated in front of peers, so that readers support the school's decision to cancel public performances like the recital
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Ruth's mistake occurs in a private lesson, no humiliation before peers is described, and the writer never endorses canceling the recital.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the overarching thesis of the passage?

options.text: Professional musicians differ from amateur players chiefly because years of practice have allowed them to stop making audible mistakes during performance
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage states professionals 'are not people who have stopped making mistakes'; expertise lies in how they hear errors.

options.text: Because beginners cannot yet diagnose the causes of their own errors, adults who start an instrument late are unlikely to persist long enough to become fluent
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer concedes the diagnostic gap but insists it 'is an argument for teaching differently, not an argument that adults cannot learn.'

options.text: Community music schools should replace traditional spring recitals with weekly group sessions in which students perform deliberate errors for one another
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Wrong Note Wednesdays is one illustrative practice in paragraph 5, and the writer explicitly refuses to 'overstate what a Wednesday can do.'

options.text: Adult learners abandon instruments not because they make mistakes but because they hear mistakes as judgments of themselves, a habit that teaching can change
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 1 through 3 establish that students leave without failing and that the verdict/information distinction explains why; paragraphs 4 through 6 argue teachers can train the alternative hearing.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's admission that the distinction is "easier to say than to do" primarily functions to

options.text: narrow the central claim so that it applies only to students who already possess the ear needed to diagnose their own errors in real time
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Rather than restricting the claim to skilled students, the paragraph extends it to beginners by assigning the diagnostic work to the teacher.

options.text: concede that the verdict-versus-information distinction, while useful to professionals, offers little practical guidance to the adult learners it was meant to help
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer admits beginners cannot apply the distinction alone but does not abandon it for them; the teacher supplies the translation 'until the student learns the grammar.'

options.text: acknowledge that beginners cannot yet read the information in their mistakes and then redirect that limitation into a responsibility for teachers
options.label: correct
options.why: The concession (beginners lack the skill to read a flat note) is followed by 'But the gap is an argument for teaching differently' and the demand that teachers translate aloud.

options.text: grant that adults who begin late will usually quit, so that the writer's later proposal appears modest and realistic rather than overly ambitious
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly rejects the idea that the gap shows 'adults cannot learn.'

items.stem: The primary function of the first paragraph in the passage as a whole is to

options.text: preview the deliberate-mistake exercise that the writer will later recommend as a solution to the dropout problem

options.text: establish the occasion for the essay and pose the puzzle that the remaining paragraphs set out to explain

options.text: criticize the school's administrators for canceling the recital rather than addressing the reasons students were leaving

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's reference to "a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page" most directly serves to

options.text: extend the argument to readers who are not learners themselves but who shape the conditions in which a learner meets failure

set.title: The Silent Player: Watching a Conductor at Work
paragraphs: Conductors are interesting and there are many things to say about them.
For our music-history project, I spent three Thursday rehearsals watching Maestra Ilse Okonkwo-Dahl lead the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra.
She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound at all.
Before the first rehearsal, the principal cellist told me that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton.
At the second rehearsal, I watched Okonkwo-Dahl inhale sharply just before the opening chord of the overture the group was learning, and all forty players came in together.
Later, when she forgot to breathe before the same chord, the entrance was ragged.
Conductors always control everything that happens in a performance.
In the third rehearsal, Okonkwo-Dahl stopped the brass section four times in ten minutes.
Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around, but she never raised her voice.
She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer, which was a thing that happened each time she did the hand thing, and it was pretty awesome to see.
In the end, conductors are a big deal.

set.title: Forty Lengths at Harrow Street
paragraphs: Every summer since I was fourteen, I have spent my mornings at the Harrow Street Pool in Calder Falls, first as a swimmer and now as a lifeguard.
Pools are important to communities in many ways.
At six in the morning, the lap lanes belong to retirees like Mr. Okafor, who swims exactly forty lengths and then tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself.
By noon, the shallow end fills with day-camp kids whose counselors call out names in four languages.
The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet.
Last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from the apartments on Delmont Avenue how to float on her back, his hand flat beneath her spine until she no longer needed it.
Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money.
Everyone in town agreed that this was a terrible idea.
I spoke at the budget hearing, holding a petition with 312 signatures I had collected at the snack bar.
The council kept the pool open, but it cut the evening hours, the only time many working parents could bring their children.
That decision was totally lame, and honestly it bugged me a lot.

What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that a public space only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up for it in the places where the decisions about it get made.
In conclusion, swimming is a very good form of exercise for people of all ages.

set.title: Who Holds Up the Trail?
paragraphs: Most people who hike the Tamsett Trail never think about who put the trail there.
The 140-mile path that crosses the hills above our town was not carved by nature or by a government agency.
It was built, and is still kept open, by volunteers with shovels.
Building a trail is slower than most people imagine.
A crew first flags a route with orange ribbon, choosing a line that climbs gently so rain will not turn the path into a creek.
Then they cut back brush, dig out the tread with heavy hoes called pulaskis, and set stone steps where the slope is too steep.
Last October, a crew of twelve spent an entire Saturday finishing just forty feet of trail near Bramble Gap.
Maintenance never ends.
Every winter, storms knock trees across the path and wash out the drainage ditches the crews dug.
The Tamsett Trail Association says it needs at least sixty volunteers each spring to clear the damage.
Last year only thirty-one showed up.
Honestly, if you're not out there you're kind of being lazy, so get off the couch.
The spring crew day is April 19, volunteers meet at the Ridge Road trailhead at 8 a.m.
Gloves, tools, and lunch are provided.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that gives evidence the volunteer shortfall actually harmed the trail. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The volunteers who did come cleared the overlook at Bramble Gap, where hikers can see four counties on a clear day.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Describes work that got done, which suggests the shortfall did little harm.

options.text: The number of hikers using the trail on summer weekends has grown steadily over the past several years.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Relates to the trail in general but gives no evidence of damage caused by the missing volunteers.

options.text: As a result, a two-mile stretch below Corbin Ridge stayed blocked by fallen trees until the middle of August.
options.label: correct
options.why: Shows a specific, concrete consequence of the shortfall, supporting the claim that too few volunteers hurt the trail.

options.text: Everyone knows that a trail without enough volunteers will eventually fall apart and disappear completely.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: An overstated generalization with no specific evidence of actual harm.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a comparison after sentence 7 that helps readers who have never done trail work picture how little forty feet is. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A pulaski is a tool with an axe blade on one side and a digging blade on the other side.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Defines a tool instead of making the distance concrete, and sentence 6 already introduces the pulaski.

options.text: Other long trails in the region are even longer than the Tamsett, some stretching hundreds of miles.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Compares whole trail lengths, which does nothing to make forty feet of progress vivid.

options.text: I hiked that section myself in November and noticed how smooth and even the new path felt underfoot.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Adds a personal detail about the section but does not help readers grasp the small size of forty feet.

options.text: That is about the length of the hallway outside our cafeteria, a walk that takes most of us ten seconds.
options.label: correct
options.why: Compares forty feet to a familiar school space, so readers can feel how small one full day's progress is.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that it urges classmates to volunteer with an encouraging, respectful tone. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Participation in volunteer maintenance activities is hereby recommended to all members of the student body.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stiff and bureaucratic, it sounds like an official notice instead of an encouraging appeal from a peer.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who skips crew day is just proving they care more about their phones than about anything real.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insults the readers, keeping the hostile tone the revision is supposed to remove.

options.text: Maybe come if you feel like it, though it is totally fine if you would rather sleep in that Saturday.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Friendly, but it undercuts the urgency the editorial needs after the shortfall it has just described.

options.text: The trail depends on people like us, and a single Saturday of our work can make a real difference.
options.label: correct
options.why: Urges action respectfully and includes the writer among the readers, which suits an appeal to classmates.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a closing sentence after sentence 14 that eases the worry of classmates who have never done outdoor work and ends with a clear call to join the crew. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: No experience is needed, because crew leaders teach every task on the spot, so bring a friend and come help keep the trail open.
options.label: correct
options.why: It speaks directly to newcomers' lack of experience with a reassuring detail and closes with a specific invitation to volunteer.

options.text: The Tamsett Trail Association has kept the path open for many years, and its crews have rebuilt dozens of washed-out sections.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It gives background on the association but neither calms newcomers' worries nor asks readers to come.

options.text: Experienced hikers who already know how to swing a pulaski will find the spring crew day especially rewarding this year.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It speaks to experienced volunteers, which may make students with no outdoor experience feel even more out of place.

options.text: Trail work can be dangerous and exhausting, so only students in excellent physical shape should think about signing up.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It discourages the same newcomers the writer is trying to recruit, which works against the editorial's persuasive purpose.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it moves smoothly from building a trail (paragraph 2) to maintaining it, making clear that the work goes on after construction is finished. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Yet finishing a stretch of trail is only the beginning, because maintenance never ends.
options.label: correct
options.why: It connects the finished construction to the ongoing upkeep and shows that the work continues after building.

options.text: As a result of this slow building process, maintenance never ends.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: It wrongly says slow construction causes the endless maintenance, when winter storms are the cause.

options.text: Similarly, building a trail with pulaskis never ends either.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It stays on building rather than moving to maintenance, so it does not make the shift the paragraph needs.

options.text: For instance, the crew near Bramble Gap had maintenance problems.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It presents an example the draft never gives and does not state the general point that upkeep is ongoing.
